# Method-of-Moment estimation

The program here will be comprised of sampling
from a known distribution, using the Method of
Moments to obtain an estimate $\hat\theta$ of
parameter $\theta$, and generating a simulated
sampling distribution for $\hat\theta$.

## Normal population, with $mu=20, \sigma=2$

First, we note that $\bar X$ is $\hat\mu$.
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| warning: false
manyXbars = replicate(10000, {xvals = rnorm(50,20,2); mean(~xvals)})
gf_dhistogram(~manyXbars) |>
  gf_vline(xintercept=20)
mean(~manyXbars)   # note the nearness to 20
```
This histogram gives the **sampling distribution
of the sample mean** (or a simulation thereof),
where

 * iid random samples are drawn from Norm$(20,2)$
 * all samples are of size $n=50$
 
The mean of the sampling distribution of $\bar
X$---that is, $E(\bar X)$---is computed as
`{r} mean(~manyXbars)`
which is very close to the mean $\mu=20$ of the
population, confirming that $\bar X$ is an
unbiased estimator of the population mean $\mu$.

**Q:** Is this true merely because our population,
in the last go, was *normal*?  Let's try a
non-normal population.

## An exponential population with rate parameter
$\lambda=0.5$

The mean $\mu = \frac{1}{\lambda} = 2$.  We
determined the method-of-moments estimator of
$\lambda$ is $\hat\lambda = \frac{1}{\bar X}$.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| warning: false
manyXbars = replicate(10000, mean(~rexp(50,0.5)))
gf_dhistogram(~manyXbars) |>
  gf_vline(xintercept=2)
mean(~manyXbars)   # note the nearness to 2
```

Again, the sample mean appears to be an unbiased
estimator of $\mu = \frac{1}{\lambda}$.
 
## Exploring if $\hat\mu_2'$ is an unbiased of variance $\sigma^2$

Recall that $v = \frac{1}{n}\sum (X_i-\bar X)$
is a the method-of-moment estimator of $\sigma^2$.
Below, I return to sampling from a normal
population.
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
#| warning: false
manyVs = replicate(100000, 49/50 * var(~rnorm(50, 20, 2)))
gf_dhistogram(~manyVs) |>
  gf_vline(xintercept=4, color="blue") |>
  gf_vline(xintercept=mean(~manyVs), color="red")
mean(~manyVs)
```

The value of the variance, $\sigma^2=4$, is
highlighted with the blue vertical line.
It is a bit to the right of the mean of the
simulated sampling distribution of $v$ (at the
red vertical line), the value `{r} mean(~manyVs)`,
suggesting that $v$ is *not* an unbiased estimator
of $\sigma^2$. Verification of this can be done
through direct calculation, but some details
are technical.  The result, however, is
$$ \mbox{E}(v) \;=\; \mbox{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}
 \sum_i (X_i-\bar X)^2\right] \;=\;
 \cdots \;=\; \frac{n-1}{n} \sigma^2, $$
not $\sigma^2$.
